matching.reasoningTemplate: Miosis, hypersalivation and bradycardia after exposure suggest organophosphate poisoning.

clinicalPearls: Belongs to the depressed physiologic state / cholinergic toxidrome; miosis is common and is most pronounced in opioid and cholinergic poisoning, distinguished from other depressant syndromes by muscarinic and nicotinic signs (p.3705).

Muscarinic features: seizures, excessive secretions (lacrimation, salivation, bronchorrhoea and wheezing, diaphoresis), and increased bowel/bladder activity with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, and incontinence of faeces and urine (p.3712).
Nicotinic features: hypertension, tachycardia, muscle cramps, fasciculations, weakness, and paralysis — note these oppose the muscarinic picture, so vital signs can be mixed (p.3712).
Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712).
Organophosphates and carbamates can produce bradycardia and atrioventricular block on ECG (p.3706).
Organophosphate (and amanita/mushroom) poisoning can present as acute, often systemic-compromising diarrhoea (p.46/Acute Diarrhea chapter).
Organophosphates can cause a delayed organophosphate-induced neuropathy: early generalised weakness from neuromuscular blockade, then an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy ensues (p.3610).
harrison.pathophysiology: Organophosphate (and carbamate) insecticides, and nerve agents such as sarin, soman, tabun and VX, inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to accumulation of synaptic acetylcholine at both muscarinic and nicotinic cholinergic receptor sites; the resulting overstimulation produces the combined muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS toxidrome. Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' in that they may require metabolic activation, so onset of toxicity can be delayed. Separately, organophosphates bind and inhibit neuropathy target esterase, with axonal degeneration of the gracile fasciculus and corticospinal tracts producing a delayed sensorimotor polyneuropathy. (p.3610, p.3712, p.3704)
additionalDifferentials: Carbamate insecticide poisoning (aldicarb, carbaryl, propoxur) — same cholinergic mechanism (p.3712)
Other acetylcholinesterase inhibitors: medicinal agents neostigmine, physostigmine, tacrine (p.3712)
Muscarinic agonists: bethanechol, pilocarpine, and muscarine-containing mushrooms (Boletus, Clitocybe, Inocybe spp.) (p.3712)
Opioid poisoning (also causes miosis and physiologic depression) (p.3705)
nonInfectiousMimics: Guillain-Barré syndrome / acute flaccid paralysis — organophosphate, thallium and arsenic poisonings are listed in the GBS differential (p.3620)
Botulism and myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular junction disorders in the acute paralysis differential) (p.3620)
Paralytic shellfish poisoning, ciguatera, type E botulism and tetrodotoxin poisoning — organophosphate poisoning is in their shared differential (ciguatera chapter)
additionalInvestigations: Cholinesterase activity in plasma and red cells is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning (p.3712)
ECG — may show bradycardia and atrioventricular block (p.3706)
EMG/nerve conduction studies in delayed neuropathy — early repetitive firing of CMAPs and decrement on repetitive nerve stimulation; later, axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy (p.3610)
redFlags: Bronchorrhoea, wheezing and excessive secretions with progression to respiratory failure — the usual cause of death (p.3712)
harrison.prognosis: Death is usually due to respiratory failure (p.3712). Outcome and reversibility of any poisoning depend on the functional reserve of the individual or target organ, influenced by age and preexisting disease (p.3704).
pitfalls: Vital signs may be discordant: muscarinic effects cause bradycardia while nicotinic stimulation can cause hypertension and tachycardia, so a 'normal' or mixed heart rate does not exclude poisoning (p.3712).
Organophosphates are 'toxic time-bombs' requiring metabolic activation, so a patient may be initially well or minimally symptomatic and deteriorate later (p.3704).
Cholinesterase activity is <50% of normal in acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning — a key confirmatory threshold not to overlook (p.3712).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison grades poisoning by degree of physiologic depression rather than by a disease-specific scale: grade 1 — arousable by voice/touch, can converse and follow commands; grade 2 — responds to pain but not voice, brainstem reflexes intact; grade 3 — unresponsive to pain, brainstem reflexes depressed, decreased respirations and temperature; grade 4 — flaccid paralysis with absent brainstem reflexes and respirations and decreased cardiovascular vital signs (p.3705).
